messages.subject: Kriging Model
parts:
Hi All,

I am trying to implement a Kriging model that was written by Brad Carlin. I think that it runs ok in JAGS, but I would like to port it over to stan.  Attached is a R file that contains both rjags and rstan code of my attempt to get this working.

There is trouble toward the bottom of the stan model, when I try to do a dot_product and also when I try a multi_normal function.  I know it's a lot to ask of the group to debug my code, but I am sufficiently confused with the differences between BUGS and stan that I have no choice but to ask.

Best regards,

Eric

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Kriging Model
parts:
You're mixing scalars and vectors and arrays. For instance,

for( n in 1:N )
W[n] ~ multi_normal(muW[n], Omega[n]);

Omega is a single covariance matrix so Omega[n] is referring to a
single column of omega and muW is an array of N scalars so muW[n] is
just a single scalar. Same with W[n] and X[n] in the dot product
line. Perhaps you just want:

W ~ multi_normal(muW,Omega);


Also beyond those issues, your line:

for( n in 1:N )
mu[n] ~ dot_product(X[n],beta) + W[n];

doesn't make sense. ~ must always have a distribution on the right
hand side, not a statement. If you're trying to assign something to
mu[n] then you need to use <- and, in this case, you can't because mu
is a parameter. If you want it saved, then you should make mu a
transformed parameter. Otherwise, you should just make it a local
variable.

Hopefully this helps!

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Kriging Model
parts:
It looks like beta should be in the parameters, not transformed
parameters, block as it's never set in there.

Also, why are you only ever using the first column of X and the first
entry of beta? Perhaps you mean:

mu <- X * beta + W

where you change the types to be:

vector[N] mu;
vector[p] beta;

You never actually use those other entries otherwise.

Regarding the negative scale parameters, you need to constrain
errorprec and spatprec to be positive. E.G.,

real<lower=0> errorprec;

Also, your last line is using the precision parameter, but the normal
distribution takes a standard deviation parameter. That line could
also be made much faster. E.G., just write

Y ~ normal(mu,sqrt(errsq));

instead of the for loop. This takes advantage of vectorization
internally. Not a huge point, but it will be a big difference in
speed for large N.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Kriging Model
parts:
On Wednesday, October 31, 2012 1:28:44 PM UTC-4, Marcus wrote:
Also, your last line is using the precision parameter, but the normal
distribution takes a standard deviation parameter.

Also, the multivariate normal distribution in BUGS is parameterized in terms of the precision matrix, whereas in Stan it is parameterized in terms of the covariance matrix. So, instead of

W ~ multi_normal(muW, Omega);

you should do

W ~ multi_normal(muW, H);

and not even define Omega.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Kriging Model
parts:
On Wednesday, October 31, 2012 3:18:16 PM UTC-4, eric.c.brown wrote:
Great tip, Ben!!!!!   Here's my (our) final code, which seems to give the same answer between JAGS and Stan.

I'm surprised that the answers are largely similar because you still have one mistake:

Y ~ normal(mu,sqrt(errorprec));

should be

Y ~ normal(mu, 1.0/sqrt(errorprec));

As Marcus said, Stan parameterizes the normal distribution in terms of the standard deviation. You also have a transformed parameter, tausq, that is not used. If you care about those, you should move them to a generated quantities block at the end.

There are some additional optimizations that you can do, in particular vectorizing more Gaussians. This is how I would do it, using what we call the multivariate Matt trick (Terrance Savitsky's models on stan-users also utilize this a lot) to write a multivariate normal vector in terms of a Cholesky factor and i.i.d. standard normals.

data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> p;
  real Y[N];
matrix[N,p] X;

real y[N];
  real x[N];
  real d[N,N];
}
parameters {

real<lower=0> errorprec;
  real<lower=0> spatprec;
  real<lower=0.1,upper=10> phi;
  vector[N] W_z; // has a standard normal prior below
  vector[p] beta;
}
model { // I prefer to put intermediate quantities in model{} so they do not get saved
  vector[N] mu;
  real sigmasq;
  matrix[N,N] H;

  sigmasq <- 1.0/spatprec;
  for (i in 1:(N-1)) {
    H[i,i] <- sigmasq; // do not waste time with the exp(-phi * 0) -> 1
    for (j in (i+1):N) {
      H[i,j] <- sigmasq*exp(-phi*d[i,j]);
      H[j,i] <- H[i,j]; // do not calculate twice, utilize symmetry
    }
  }
  H[N,N] <- sigmasq;
 
  beta ~ normal(0,100); // vectorize this rather than looping
 
  errorprec ~ gamma(0.1,0.1);
  spatprec ~ gamma(0.1,0.1);
  // implicit:  phi ~ uniform(0.1,10);
 
  W_z ~ normal(0.0, 1.0); // 1st part of the multivariate Matt trick

  mu <- X * beta + cholesky_decompose(H) * W_z; // 2nd part of multivariate Matt trick
  Y ~ normal(mu, 1.0/sqrt(errorprec)); // with the standard deviation
}
generated quantities {
  real tausq;
  tausq <- 1.0/errorprec;
}

Ben
